 The Aesthetic Synergy of 
Korean Beauty and Style
 Cover Story 1 
 Writer 
 Alex Suh 
 This past August, a vibrant slice of Seoul came to life in Los Angeles, recreating the city’s iconic streetscape for a three-day celebration of style. As over 100,000 visitors strolled past replica bus stops and illuminated Hangeul (Korean alphabet) signage, they discovered an experience that extended far beyond cosmetics. Beyond the latest skincare innovations and makeup trends, the festival offered a captivating glimpse into the underlying philosophy of Korean self-care. This article takes a closer look at Koreans’ cultural approach to beauty and style that continues to fascinate and inspire audiences around the globe. 
 From Passing Fad to Signature Aesthetic -->
 The K-beauty festival—called OLIVE YOUNG FESTA LA 2026—was held alongside KCON LA, with 55 brands taking part. Perhaps surprisingly, the biggest draws were not seen at particular products. Instead, most people lined up at booths for personal color consultations to learn which shades suited them best and for skin analyses recommending tailored skin care regimens. In the middle of the venue stood a veritable recreation of an OLIVE YOUNG outlet from Seoul. It was less about displaying products than demonstrating a method. 
After K-pop and K-dramas paved the way for the spread of Korean culture, the first Korean beauty products to reach global audiences were sheet masks, cushion compacts and the like. Where international consumers once bought sheet masks to imitate the celebrities seen in dramas, they have now grown curious about how ordinary Koreans take care of themselves. Western makeup excels at evening skin tone and redefining facial contours. Western fashion, too, makes its presence felt through stark silhouettes and bold colors. But Korean beauty and fashion begin with a different question. Rather than asking, “How do I want to look?” they ask, “What suits me?” K-style, then, is the art not of reinvention but of refinement. Three principles underpin this approach.

 The Principles of K-beauty and K-fashion -->
 Principle #1. Cultivate a Natural Look 
There is an intriguing paradox at work here. According to OpenSurvey’s “Beauty Trend Report 2023,” the average Korean woman uses about six skincare products, compared with roughly three or four in the United States and Japan. Yet despite using nearly twice as many products, Korean consumers ultimately want their face to look like nothing has been applied to it. Koreans call this kkuankku —basically, the “no-makeup makeup” look. The ideal of K-beauty is sokgwang , a complexion that seems to glow from within. Hence the daily layering of toner, serum and sunscreen rather than reliance on heavy foundation. 
Fashion is oriented in much the same direction. The streets of Seoul’s Seongsu-dong and Hannam-dong neighborhoods—the favorite haunts of Korea’s fashion-forward crowd—are less flamboyant than Tokyo’s Shinjuku or New York’s Times Square. Coordinated tones and understated silhouettes are all the rage. It is telling, too, that one of the go-to brands for Korea’s younger consumers is not a daring designer label but Musinsa Standard, which specializes in wardrobe essentials. Underlying this sensibility is a preference for being tasteful, rather than ostentatious. It also helps explain the recent enthusiasm for “slow aging.” Rather than seeking treatments to remove wrinkles, the focus has shifted toward everyday habits that slow the aging process. The guiding belief is that good health represents style at its finest. 
 Principle #2. Assess Yourself Accurately 
If style in the West is about “being” yourself, in Korea it begins with “knowing” yourself. And the most common tool for doing that is personal color analysis. The colors of a person’s skin, hair and eyes are classified into warm or cool tones and then subdivided into four seasonal palettes. Terms such as “cool summer” have long since entered everyday vocabulary. Knowing your “season” can impact your choice of colors in everything from lipstick to knitwear. Many international visitors now travel to Seoul specifically for these consultations. 
But personal color is not the only thing to analyze. Body shape analysis identifies flattering clothing contours based on bone structure and musculature. The ingredient-analysis app Hwahae helps users distinguish beneficial cosmetic ingredients from those that are best avoided. Reviews on online fashion platforms routinely include buyers’ heights and weights. All these tools serve the same purpose: finding the shades and fits that suit you just as you are. In a sense, they allow everyone to become the designer of their own personal style. 
 Principle #3. Document and Share Your Routine 
These first two principles are made possible by the habit of keeping records. Many people document everything from their morning and evening skin care routines to their daily outfits. Video platforms are awash with clips focusing less on the finished look than on the steps taken to achieve it. Online stores sometimes display tens of thousands of reviews for a single product. 
But these records function as more than a personal diary. Candid reviews—along the lines of “My skin is dry but also oily” and “It gets rid of dead skin, but leaves my skin feeling too tight”—give beauty brands clues about where to go next. A case study by the Harvard Business School found that OLIVE YOUNG jointly develops roughly 20% of its products with brands carried at its retail outlets. Users’ reviews become the blueprints for new products, which then find their way back into those same users’ daily lives. If “before and after” is the catchphrase of Western beauty, K-style valorizes the “routine.” This is the story not of a dramatic transformation, but a slow-but-steady process, and many authors have a hand in the telling of this tale.

 K-style as a Global Lifestyle
 K-style’s current direction can already be seen in the overseas ventures Korean retailers have launched since this summer. THE HYUNDAI, Hyundai Department Store’s first overseas flagship store, opened in Tokyo in July. Within two weeks of its opening, the number of visitors in their 20s and 30s to the shopping complex where it is located had increased more than fivefold. Every weekend, lines form before the doors open. In August, Musinsa launched a pop-up in Harajuku inspired by Seoul’s Seongsu-dong neighborhood. Following a similar initiative in New York, Shinsegae Department Store brought District Seoul to Shibuya in October. What all these events have in common is that they are exporting not simply Korean products, but the experience of shopping in Seoul itself. 
But stores are hardly the only things crossing borders. At OLIVE YOUNG’s Seongsu-dong branch, roughly 70% of users of its beauty experience services are from abroad. Travelers take the habits they learn in Seoul back home with them. Before long, such services may well become commonplace in cities throughout the world. There is a downside, of course. Such attention to detail, while undoubtedly exacting, can be exhausting. The next evolution of K-style will likely involve a shift toward rest and relaxation. One sign is the growing prominence of “recovery” alongside “care” in the discourse on beauty. 
What Korean beauty and fashion have brought to the world is not a particular approach to makeup or outfits. Rather, it is a different way of treating oneself. Touch up, rather than cover up; redesign, rather than redefine. That is the grammar of K-style.
 Writer Alex Suh 
Alex Suh researches consumer culture in Korea and the wider world. A co-author of the “Trend Korea” series and books on K-beauty trends, Suh has worked on consumer insight projects with such companies as Samsung Electronics, Amorepacific and LG Electronics.

 The Future of Korean Hospitality 
 The global hospitality industry continues moving toward the same shared priorities: luxury, wellness, digital transformation and sustainability. However, Korea’s competitive edge does not lie in being the first to adopt these trends. Instead, it stems from blending global influences with Korean lifestyle culture to create a uniquely compelling narrative. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) has also stressed that the future of tourism competitiveness will depend on how well locality, digital innovation and sustainability can be woven together. 
The direction Korea’s lodging industry should take going forward is clear: not supplying more rooms, but offering deeper experiences. Hotels need to become platforms that connect local ingredients, artisan craftsmanship, art, design and the everyday lives of residents—organically weaving together Hanok and local stays, wellness, fine dining and K-culture to create a lodging experience possible only in Korea. 
For international visitors, too, a night in Korea is unlikely to remain just a place to sleep. The Seoul skyline glimpsed through a hotel window at night, morning light filtering in beneath a Hanok’s eaves or a day that begins at a small bakery down the alley—these are glimpses of Korea that sightseeing alone could never offer. 
If hotels around the world sell rooms, Korea today offers something else: time to experience a way of life. That is precisely why Korean hospitality is drawing global attention right now, and it will likely remain the industry’s greatest competitive edge going forward. 
 Writer. Seo HyunJin 
Seo HyunJin is the Editor-in-Chief of Hotel & Restaurant, a global hospitality magazine founded in 1991.

 From Watching to Doing
 Korea’s sports wave has moved well beyond the stadium and into daily life. The baseball boom has triggered an amateur league explosion—booking a weekend diamond has become nearly impossible. Tennis, golf and a years-long running crew trend have become defining lifestyle markers for younger Koreans. 
Rising health consciousness and a declining drinking culture have transformed sports from spectator entertainment into a full-blown cultural phenomenon. Elite and recreational sports now reinforce each other in a virtuous cycle that has the sportswear and equipment industries booming as well. After K-pop, K-drama and K-food, K-sports is now showing real potential as a global cultural phenomenon. 
Once you experience K-sports, you won’t forget it. Now it’s your turn to become part of that passion. 
 Writer. Han Sung-yun 
Han joined KBS in 1997 as a sports reporter. He received a commendation from the Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism in 2017 and won the SoKang Sports Journalism Award in 2019. He has authored multiple books on sports culture.

 Toward a Global Standard
 Building on this success, the “K-convenience store system” is now being exported—not merely as a way to stock Korean products on foreign shelves, but as a wholesale transplant of store design, operating systems and convenience store culture. International locations surpassed 1,500 as of 2025, and in countries like Mongolia and Vietnam, K-convenience stores have become beloved gathering spots where young locals go to experience Korean culture firsthand. 
The trajectory is clear: Korean convenience stores are moving beyond an oversaturated domestic market to set a new global standard. The differentiation strategies and technological capabilities honed in one of the world’s most competitive retail environments are reshaping what convenience retail can look like—and K-convenience stores look set to become a fixture in the daily lives of people far beyond Korea’s borders. 
 Writer. Dahye Han 
Han is a research fellow at the Consumer Trend Analysis Center of Trend Korea and co-author of the bestselling “Trend Korea” series. She holds a BA in Psychology from Seoul National University, where she also completed her master’s and doctoral studies in Consumer Studies. She conducts consumer trend and future strategy research for companies including Samsung, SK and LG, and has co-authored “K-Beauty Trends,” “Twenty-One Thirty-Nine” and the “Korea Food Service Industry Trends” series. She teaches at Seoul National University at both the undergraduate and graduate levels, appears regularly on KBS1 Radio, and delivers consumer trend-related lectures at a wide range of corporations.
